title: Stephen Hawking: When Black Holes Glow
source_book: Black hole explosions? (Nature, Vol. 248) & A Brief History of Time
source_chapter: Nature 248, 30–31 (1 March 1974) & Chapter 7: Black Holes Ain't So Black
authenticity_note: Directly derived from Stephen Hawking's revolutionary 1974 Nature paper combining quantum field theory and general relativity to prove that black holes emit thermal radiation and can slowly evaporate.
summary: Battling motor neuron disease and doing complex tensor calculations entirely in his mind, Stephen Hawking combined Einstein's general relativity with quantum mechanics. He discovered that black holes are not completely black—quantum vacuum fluctuations near the event horizon cause black holes to emit thermal glow, now known as 'Hawking Radiation'.
content:
In the early 1970s, prevailing scientific dogma held that black holes were the ultimate cosmic dead ends. Formed when massive stars collapsed under their own ferocious gravity, a black hole was bounded by an 'event horizon'—a one-way boundary from which nothing, not even light itself traveling at 300,000 kilometers per second, could ever escape. Whatever fell into a black hole was lost forever, and its mass could only increase.

Young British physicist Stephen Hawking, already severely paralyzed by Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and confined to a wheelchair, turned his sharp intellect to this paradox. Unable to write equations by hand, Hawking developed extraordinary mental visualization techniques, manipulating complex geometric shapes and four-dimensional tensor equations in his head.

Hawking decided to investigate what happens when the weird laws of quantum mechanics are applied to the razor-thin boundary of a black hole's event horizon.

According to quantum field theory, 'empty space' is not empty at all. It seethes with quantum fluctuations—virtual particle-antiparticle pairs constantly popping into existence from the vacuum, colliding, and annihilating each other in a trillionth of a second.

Hawking asked: What happens if such a particle-antiparticle pair pops into existence right on the brink of the event horizon?

Before the pair can recombine and annihilate, one member of the pair falls inward across the event horizon, trapped forever! The other member of the pair is left stranded outside with no partner to annihilate. To conserve total energy, the escaping particle streams away into deep space as real radiation—carrying positive energy away from the black hole!

To an outside observer, the black hole appears to glow with steady thermal energy! Because the escaping particle takes energy away, the black hole must steadily lose mass. Over astronomical timescales, black holes do not grow forever—they slowly simmer, evaporate, and eventually vanish in a final burst of gamma rays.

Hawking's 1974 discovery of **Hawking Radiation** shook theoretical physics to its foundations, forging the very first mathematical bridge between Einstein's General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics.

The boundary defining the region of space around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape.
The temporary random appearance of particle-antiparticle pairs from empty space due to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.
The theoretical process by which a black hole slowly loses mass and eventually explodes due to Hawking radiation.
